reference.source: Rook's Textbook of Dermatology / Fitzpatrick's Dermatology
clinicalPearls: The acute pole of the pityriasis lichenoides spectrum, marked by abrupt crops of erythematous papules that vesiculate, become haemorrhagic or necrotic, and crust over
Individual lesions may heal with varioliform (smallpox-like) pitted scars, unlike the chronic PLC form
Successive crops mean lesions at different stages of evolution are present at the same time
Predominantly affects children and young adults, favouring the trunk and proximal limbs
Usually benign and self-limiting but tends to run a more inflammatory and relapsing course than PLC
The rare febrile ulceronecrotic Mucha-Habermann variant presents with high fever, large coalescing necrotic ulcers, and systemic symptoms and can be life-threatening
Biopsy shows a dense, often wedge-shaped lymphocytic infiltrate with interface change, keratinocyte necrosis, and extravasated red cells

Managed with topical corticosteroids, oral antibiotics with anti-inflammatory action (such as tetracyclines or macrolides), and phototherapy, with systemic immunosuppression reserved for the ulceronecrotic variant
reference.pathophysiology: PLEVA is regarded as a reactive, predominantly CD8-positive cytotoxic T-cell response that produces a lymphocytic vasculitis and epidermal injury. As with the chronic form, triggers are thought to include infectious antigens and, in some cases, drugs, which provoke an inflammatory cascade damaging both keratinocytes and dermal vessels. The intense cytotoxic reaction accounts for the vesiculation, haemorrhage, and necrosis of individual lesions and for the varioliform scarring that can follow. In the severe febrile ulceronecrotic variant an exaggerated response, sometimes with a large clonal T-cell population and cytokine release, drives widespread ulceration and systemic illness.
additionalInvestigations: Skin biopsy for histopathology to demonstrate the cytotoxic interface reaction with necrosis
T-cell receptor gene rearrangement studies and immunophenotyping to exclude lymphomatoid papulosis
Viral swabs or PCR for varicella-zoster or herpes simplex where a vesicular infection is suspected
Full blood count, inflammatory markers, and close observation for systemic upset in suspected febrile ulceronecrotic disease
Serology for potential triggers (Epstein-Barr virus, Toxoplasma, HIV) when indicated
Blood cultures if the patient is febrile and systemically unwell
redFlags: High fever with rapidly enlarging, coalescing necrotic ulcers indicating febrile ulceronecrotic Mucha-Habermann disease
Systemic features such as arthralgia, abdominal pain, or mucosal involvement
Extensive necrosis raising the risk of secondary infection and sepsis
Atypical or clonal lymphoid infiltrate suggesting lymphomatoid papulosis or lymphoma
reference.prognosis: Most cases resolve over weeks to months, though relapses are common and varioliform scarring may persist; the febrile ulceronecrotic variant carries appreciable morbidity and, rarely, mortality and warrants urgent aggressive treatment.
pitfalls: Misdiagnosing early vesicular lesions as chickenpox and missing the relapsing crop pattern
Failing to recognise and treat the febrile ulceronecrotic variant promptly
Overlooking the clinical and histological overlap with lymphomatoid papulosis
Attributing residual varioliform scars to another cause
